To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) the pixels are diverse, (b) the pixels should represent themselves, and (c) the pixels should be trained tabula rasa.

(1) stratified sampling of the pixels can be used to improve the performance of a convolutional neural network for pixel-level prediction problems; (2) the resulting model can be trained from scratch for different tasks, such as semantic segmentation, surface normal estimation, and edge detection; (3) our model achieves the state-of-the-art performance for each of these tasks; (4) the model has fewer than 10M parameters and can run in real-time on a GPU.

(1) stratified sampling of the pixels allows one to train state-of-the- art models tabula rása (i.e., from scratch) for diverse pixel-level prediction problems; (2) the proposed PixelNet architecture is a generic and efficient solution for pixel-level prediction; and (3), the proposed PixelNet model is the first model to achieve state-of-the-art performance for diverse pixel-level tasks, including semantic segmentation, surface normal estimation, and edge detection.

the question of how to learn from pixels.
the representation of pixels by the pixels, for the pixels.
the question of how to learn to predict the pixels, by learning from the pixels, and in turn to improve the pixels.

, by exploiting the redundancy of the pixels through stratified sampling, we can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy with a single architecture, while speeding up the learning process.
we have shown how to learn pixel-level prediction tasks from scratch with a single model and a single loss function, while achieving state-of-the-art accuracy.

The main takeaway from our work is that
convolutional processing is not necessary for pixel-level prediction problems.
the design of convolutional predictors should be guided by statistical efficiency, rather than computational efficiency.
the design of a pixel-level prediction architecture should be guided by statistical principles, rather than by the desire to exploit spatial redundancy.
